title: Rush lampshade liner
subtitle: Basketry: a woven rush panel fitted inside a wire lampshade frame
excerpt: A woven rush panel worked flat and then fitted to the inside of a standard wire drum lampshade frame. The rush weave diffuses the light and gives the shade a warm natural texture. Worked in natural dried rush using a simple randing weave on a temporary board loom.
sourceNotes: Twining, Basketwork for Beginners (1920) for the flat rush weave panel technique; Cassell's Book of the Household (1890) for lampshade frame lining method.

glossaryTerms.definition: Dried stems of Scirpus lacustris (bulrush) or Juncus effusus (soft rush), used in coiled and woven basketry. Must be dampened before use to prevent snapping.
Simple weaving pattern: one strand worked alternately under and over the warp stakes.
The fixed strands in a weave, running in one direction; the weavers (weft) pass over and under these.

content.text: A rush lampshade liner is a woven flat panel that wraps around the inside of a drum lampshade wire frame. The panel is woven slightly wider than the frame circumference, wrapped around and tied at the overlap. The result diffuses light through the woven structure in a pattern of warm spots rather than glowing uniformly, the effect depends on the weave density.
Fire safety.

Natural rush is combustible. This liner is designed for use with LED bulbs only, which produce minimal heat. Do not fit this liner to a shade used with incandescent or halogen bulbs, the heat output can ignite dry rush. Keep the bulb at least 15 cm below the top ring of the shade.
What you need
Natural dried rush: enough to weave a panel the height of your shade (typically 20, 25 cm) and the circumference + 5 cm (typically 95 cm). About 200 g of dried rush.
A drum lampshade wire frame, standard 30 cm diameter.
A temporary board loom: a piece of MDF or plywood slightly larger than the panel, with nails or screws set in two rows to hold the warp.
Bodkin and side cutters.
Prepare the rush
Dried
rush

must be dampened before weaving: lay the rush in a flat bundle, wrap in a damp cloth, and leave for 1, 2 hours. The rush should be flexible but not wet, it should bend around a finger without snapping. Do not submerge rush in water; it goes mushy.
Set up the board loom
Set nails in two rows at the top and bottom of the board, spaced 8 mm apart across the width of the panel. Thread the
warp
rush strands from top nail to bottom nail, pulling each strand taut. Use rush with the stems doubled for the warp, a single strand will stretch and the panel will be floppy.
Weave the panel
Use single rush strands as the weft, working in simple
randing

: under one warp strand, over the next, all the way across. On the return pass, start with the opposite sequence. Use the bodkin to push each weft row firmly toward the previous one. Maintain consistent tension, the panel should be tight but not distorted.
Remove from loom and fit

When the panel is complete, carefully remove it from the loom by lifting the warp strands off the nails. Trim the warp ends to 2 cm. Wrap the panel around the inside of the lampshade frame, overlapping the ends by 3 cm. Tie the overlap at top and bottom with a length of rush twisted into cord, thread through the weave at the overlap and knot firmly.

attrs.symptom: The panel is wavy and uneven rather than flat
attrs.cause: Weft tension varied across the rows, some rows were packed more tightly than others
attrs.fix: Use a wide flat-faced comb or a ruler to push each weft row to a consistent spacing before the rush dries. Pack rows at 8, 10 per cm for a medium-density shade.
